newsitem.title: CROATIA: Thousands celebrate Croatian Radio 101 survival.
newsitem.headline: Thousands celebrate Croatian Radio 101 survival.

text.p: Thousands of people gathered in Zagreb's main square on Thursday to celebrate the victory of an influential independent radio station against government attempts to shut it down.

Over 100,000 people, many holding candles and banners, crammed into Ban Jelacic square and its converging streets in the biggest public rally Croatia has seen since it broke away from federal Yugoslavia in 1991.
The state-controlled telecommunications council on Wednesday had awarded the popular Radio 101's frequency to a rival which does not yet exist.
Radio 101 had been a thorn in the rightist government's side for criticising the ruling nationalist HDZ party.
After the decision was made public, widespread protests -- some from Western governments -- forced the telecommunications council on Thursday to open a new tender for the radio frequency it withdrew.
Thursday's rally, watched closely by hundreds of plain-clothes and uniformed policemen ended peacefully after an hour and half.
"We won't give up sex, 101 and rock'n'roll," one banner proclaimed.
A popular rock singer publicly pledged to record a support song for Radio 101 the next day.

Earlier in the day, the United States and Britain sharply criticised the Zagreb government's move against the radio which will continue its regular broadcasting until the council reaches a new decision.
"This development in the case of Radio 101 constitutes a significant setback for democratisation and free expression in Croatia," said U.S. State Department spokesman Glyn Davies.
The owner of a rival station which obtained Radio 101's frequency, taken aback by the avalanche of protests, said in a statement he was renouncing the concession in favour of Radio 101.
"This may not be a victory of democracy but it's a definitive step towards victory," Vlado Gotovac, leader of the main opposition party, the Social Liberals, told Reuters.
Radio 101, founded in 1984, was one of the prime promoters of peaceful changes that led to the country's first democratic elections in April, 1990.

President Franjo Tudjman won that poll and led the nation to bloody secession from Yugoslavia. Since then he has been criticised for ruling the country with an authoritarian hand, clamping down on political opponents and independent media.
In a statement following a regular cabinet session, the government said that "all conditions are met for opening a new tender to award (a broadcasting licence for the Zagreb) radio frequency".
The sudden change of mind was clearly caused by international reaction and domestic protests which grew into a wider demand for democratic reforms.
"This is an emotional outlet against the whole situation in Croatia. Radio 101 is a symbol, through which the dissatisfaction reached a boiling point," said Goran Vuletic, 40, who attended the rally.
"We don't demand freedom only for 101 but for all radio and TV stations in Croatia, for all its citizens," Gotovac told the crowd from a balcony overlooking the crowd.
